title: Thread-safe class design
idea: Designing for concurrency means deciding, for every mutable field, which class owns it and how threads may reach it without corrupting it.

analogy.text: An office whiteboard. Printed notices need no rules. A tally that anyone may edit needs one marker, passed from hand to hand.
analogy.breaks: Threads may miss each other's writes without a shared lock, volatile or atomic.

points: A race needs shared mutable state, a writer, and no synchronization between threads.
`count++` is three steps: read, add, write. Another thread can slip between.
Immutable objects and thread-confined state need no locks at all.
Shared mutable state should hide its locking inside the one class that owns it.

code: // two threads run count++ on one field

steps.caption: The field holds 5. Both threads are about to run `count++` once.
Thread A reads 5 into its own local copy.
The scheduler switches threads. B also reads 5, because A has not written anything back yet.
A adds one to its copy and gets 6.
A writes 6 back to the shared field.
B adds one to its stale 5 and also gets 6.
B writes 6 over A's 6. Two increments ran, but one is lost.
Fix: make the three steps one atomic step with a lock or `AtomicInteger`. B then waits or retries, and count ends at 7.

code.title: Thread-safe counter
code.caption: Four threads share one `HitCounter`. The class owns its locking, so callers never think about it.

walk.text: Four pool threads each record 1000 hits, split between two paths.
Wait for every task to finish, and fail loudly if they time out.
The map is `private final`: no caller can reach it without going through the class.
`merge` reads, adds and writes as one atomic step per key.
Return a sorted copy, never the live map, so readers cannot break the invariant.

code.title: Lock ordering
code.caption: Two threads move money in opposite directions. A fixed lock order prevents deadlock. It finishes and prints a=1000 b=1000: no deadlock, and no money lost.

walk.text: Thread 1 sends a to b, thread 2 sends b to a, at the same time.
Each account carries its own lock; the field comment names what it guards.
Neither object alone can guard a two-account move, so only Bank takes the package-private lock.
Pick the lock order by id, not by argument order.
Take both locks, update both balances, then release in reverse order inside `finally`.

pitfalls: `map.put(k, map.get(k) + 1)` loses updates even on `ConcurrentHashMap`; use `merge`.
Taking two locks in argument order can deadlock; order them by a stable key.
Returning an internal mutable collection leaks it past your lock; return a copy.

options: A different count on each run
quiz.why: Each of four threads adds 500 hits per path. `merge` is atomic, so none are lost, and `TreeMap` sorts the keys.

takeaway: Give each mutable field one owner, and guard it inside that class.
